teaser: A small sheet of paper that a philosopher carried through exile and turned into the angel of history.
review_notes:
Dimensions about 31.8 x 24.2 cm.
Benjamin bought the work in Munich in 1921 for 1,000 marks.
Short quotation from Benjamin's ninth thesis “On the Concept of History” (Harry Zohn translation): “This is how one pictures the angel of history. His face is turned toward the past.” Please verify wording.
Bataille hid Benjamin's papers and the picture at the Bibliothèque nationale; Benjamin is said to have cut it from its frame before leaving Paris; it later passed via Adorno to Gershom Scholem; Scholem's widow gave it to the Israel Museum in 1987.
R. H. Quaytman's discovery (around 2015) that the sheet is mounted on an 1838 engraving of Martin Luther after Cranach; the dark border seen in the image is read as that engraving.
The number “32” in Klee's inscription read as the work's number within 1920.

lesson.text: This is an angel that does not seem able to fly. Its wings are raised like two hands in surrender. Its feet are the claws of a bird. Its head, too big for the body, is crowned with curls that look like rolled-up paper. And it is called “new”, on a sheet that looks scorched and ancient.

Paul Klee made it in 1920, in Munich, on a piece of paper about 32 by 24 centimeters, hardly bigger than a sheet of printer paper. He was 40. Two years earlier he had come home from the German army, where he spent part of the First World War varnishing airplane wings.

The title is Latin: Angelus Novus, the new angel. Klee drew dozens of angels over his life, and most are clumsy, forgetful, unfinished creatures, closer to us than to heaven. This one would have stayed a curiosity if one particular visitor had not walked into a Munich gallery the following year.
The buyer was Walter Benjamin, a 28-year-old German writer. In 1921 he paid 1,000 marks for the picture, and for the next two decades it hung wherever he lived.

Before Benjamin's story, the figure itself. Klee builds it from thin, wiry lines and a few washes of watercolor, which is paint thinned with water until it is transparent. Follow the body from top to bottom and count how many different animals seem to be in there.

lesson.title: Top to toe
lesson.text: One figure, floating in the middle of the sheet with nothing around it.

spots.title: Scroll hair
spots.text: The curls are drawn as little rolled tubes, like parchment scrolls. Some people read them as sacred texts, a head literally full of writing.

spots.title: Eyes and teeth
spots.text: Two round brown eyes look slightly past you. Below, the mouth hangs open and shows a row of small teeth. It is hard to say whether this is fear, speech or a grin.

spots.title: A wing, or a hand
spots.text: The wing ends in fingers. Raised like this, with the other one mirroring it, the gesture reads as surprise, blessing or surrender, depending on your mood.

spots.title: Tail and claws
spots.text: A fan-shaped tail and two thin legs with three-toed bird feet. There is no ground under them: the angel hangs in the air without flapping.

lesson.text: Fingers on the wings, teeth in the mouth, claws for feet: part bird, part child, part old man. Klee does not tell you how to feel about it. That openness is exactly why another mind could move in and furnish the picture with meaning.

The line has an odd quality, too. It is slightly fuzzy, and here and there the paper is dirtied by black specks and smudges that seem to have nothing to do with the drawing. They are not accidents of age. They come from the way the image was made.
Klee's method left stray black marks on the paper, away from the figure. Find the largest cluster.

spots.title: Transfer smudges
spots.text: These dark flecks appeared where Klee's hand pressed on the sheet while tracing. Wherever there was pressure, the black coating underneath printed itself onto the paper.

lesson.text: Klee invented a technique called oil transfer: he coated a sheet with black oil paint, laid it face down on clean paper, and traced a drawing on top with a needle. The line came through like carbon copy, soft and speckled.

He liked what this did. A line drawn directly can look too sure of itself. A transferred line arrives second-hand, a little blurred, with those random smudges around it, as if the image had been found and not made. Then he added watercolor on top, darkening the corners into a brown halo.

Klee kept a handwritten catalog of everything he made, year by year. The note “1920 32” beside his signature at lower right means this was the 32nd work he recorded in 1920. By the end of his life the list ran to roughly nine thousand entries.

Now back to Benjamin. In 1933 the Nazis took power and he, a Jewish intellectual, left Germany for Paris. The angel eventually followed him there. Early in 1940, with war under way, he wrote a short text about history, and in the middle of it he described this picture.

“This is how one pictures the angel of history,” he wrote. “His face is turned toward the past.” In his reading, the angel stares at the wreckage of everything that has happened. He would like to stay and repair it, but a storm blowing from Paradise has caught his wings and drives him backward into the future. That storm, Benjamin says, is what we call progress.

Go back to the open mouth and the raised wings with that in mind. Nothing in the drawing has changed, yet now the eyes look horrified and the wings look pinned open by wind. A few sentences turned a whimsical creature into one of the most quoted images of the twentieth century.

When German troops approached Paris in June 1940, Benjamin cut the picture from its frame and entrusted it, with his manuscripts, to the writer Georges Bataille, who hid them in the French national library where he worked.

Benjamin did not survive his flight. In September 1940, stopped at the Spanish border and fearing he would be handed back, he took his own life. The angel outlived him. After the war it reached his friend Gershom Scholem in Jerusalem, and Scholem's widow gave it to the Israel Museum in 1987.

The sheet had one more surprise. Around 2015 the American artist R. H. Quaytman, studying it closely, worked out what the dark strip around Klee's paper is. You can see that strip clearly in this photograph.

spots.title: The dark border
spots.text: Klee glued his sheet onto an old print, leaving its edges showing as a dark band. Quaytman identified it as an 1838 engraving of Martin Luther. Why Klee chose it, nobody knows.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: “Klee 1920 32”, written in ink on the watercolor: name, year, and the number of the work in his own catalog.

spots.title: The written title
spots.text: On the mount below, in Klee's neat handwriting: “Angelus novus”. He considered titles part of the work and often inscribed them like this.

spots.title: The chest
spots.text: A small vertical mark like a keyhole or an arrow sits in a warm orange patch at the center of the body, the brightest color on the sheet.

spots.title: Burnt corners
spots.text: Brown watercolor pooled toward the corners makes the paper look singed, as if the sheet had been through a fire before the angel appeared on it.

spots.title: The other wing
spots.text: A near mirror of the first, with stiff straight fingers. Benjamin imagined a wind so strong that the angel could no longer close these.

lesson.text: The same lines carried a joke for Klee and a catastrophe for Benjamin. What a picture means can depend on who has lived with it, and when.

quiz.question: Who bought Angelus Novus in 1921?
quiz.explanation: The writer Walter Benjamin bought it for 1,000 marks.

quiz.question: How does oil transfer work?
options: Paint is sprayed through a stencil
A drawing is traced over a sheet coated in black oil paint, printing the line below
Watercolor is pressed between two sheets
quiz.explanation: Klee traced with a needle over a blackened sheet, like carbon copy.

quiz.question: In Benjamin's text, which way does the angel of history face?
quiz.explanation: He looks back at the wreckage of the past while being blown into the future.

quiz.question: What does “1920 32” next to the signature mean?
quiz.explanation: Klee numbered every work in his own handwritten catalog.

quiz.question: What is the dark border around the sheet?
options: An old engraving of Martin Luther that Klee used as a mount
quiz.explanation: Klee mounted the drawing on an 1838 engraving, identified around 2015.

quiz.question: Where is the work today?
quiz.explanation: Scholem's widow gave it to the Israel Museum in 1987.

facts.text: The black specks scattered on the paper are damage from Benjamin's escape.
facts.explanation: They come from Klee's oil transfer method, where pressure printed stray marks.

facts.text: The angel has bird feet and visible teeth.
facts.explanation: Klee gave it three-toed claws and an open mouth with a row of teeth.

facts.text: Klee painted the picture as an illustration for Benjamin's essay.
facts.explanation: Klee made it in 1920; Benjamin wrote about it twenty years later.
